en: Netti 3.
The Section on Exposition (Niddesavāra).
Therein, the Guide (Netti) has been briefly explained.
3.1. Summary of Contents:
Gratification, danger, and escape; the fruit, the means, and the method.
The Blessed One’s command is the sustenance of the teaching for yogis;
that which was asked and that which was answered.
Whatever is the chanting of the Sutta,
and whatever is the investigation of the Sutta,
that is designated as the Mode of Conveying Investigation (Vicaya-hāra).
The ground of all the modes of conveying,
and their respective spheres of activity;
the examination of what is appropriate and inappropriate.
The "Jewel" and the "Method" have been explained.
The Victor teaches the Dhamma, and that which is the proximate cause for that Dhamma; [this is the "Causal Relation"].
Thus, up to all phenomena—
this is the Mode of Conveying the Footings.
When a single phenomenon has been stated...
Whatever phenomena are said to have a single characteristic,
all of them are so stated;
this is the mode of interpretation known as "Characteristic."
The ultimate intention, the phrasing,
the meaning, the source of the teaching,
and the connection between what precedes and what follows.
This is the fourfold method of analysis (catubyūha-hāra):
within one basis of meaning,
one seeks the remaining basis of meaning.
That which turns back toward the opposite side is called the Mode of Conveying the Conversion (Āvaṭṭa-hāra).
It consists of the teaching and its foundation.
"And it analyzes the plane"— this is the Mode of Conveying;
"in the common and the uncommon,
it is to be understood as Analysis."
When wholesome and unwholesome states are pointed out, cultivated, and abandoned,
they are transformed into their opposites.
The "Hāra" (Conveying) is called the "Parivattana" (Reversal).
However, many synonyms for a single dhamma are stated in the Sutta.
He who knows the Suttas thoroughly, O knower of the scriptures,
that is the Mode called Synonymy (Vevacana).
The Blessed One [taught] a single Dhamma...
He teaches by means of various designations;
that mode should be known as the "method of designation."
And that which is dependent origination,
the faculties, the aggregates, the elements, and the sense bases—
he who enters [into reality] by means of these, [attains the goal].
That method of exposition is called "Descent" (otaraṇa).
When a question has been answered,
it refers back to the verse from which that question was originally posed.
The investigation of the pure and the impure is the extraction known as "purification.
Of phenomena, by way of their unity—
And those things which have been demonstrated as being diverse should not be conceptualized;
this is the Mode of Conveying Determination.
Whatever phenomena produce another phenomenon through successive conditions,
having drawn out the cause—
This is the Mode of Conveying, the Requisite.
Those phenomena which have a particular root,
and those which are shown by the Sage to have a single meaning;
They are to be applied;
this is the Mode of Conveying Application (samāropana-hāra).
3.2. Summary of Methods (naya-saṅkhepa)
He who leads both craving and ignorance by means of serenity and insight,
having joined them with the truths—
This method is the "turning of the joy" (nandiyāvaṭṭa).
It leads one from the unwholesome by means of its roots,
and to the wholesome by means of the wholesome roots.
That which is real, true, and not false—
this they call the Tipukkhala method;
it is that which leads one away from the perversions.
Defilements, faculties, and true states—
those who know the method call this the "Lion’s Play" method.
Indeed, whatever wholesome and unwholesome [states] are spoken of here and there in the analytical expositions (veyyākaraṇa),
one should examine them with the mind.
That indeed they call "surveying the directions.
Having surveyed with the vision of the directions,
one raises [the mind] and brings it back to composure.
"All wholesome and unwholesome states"—
this method is called the "hook.
The sixteen modes of conveying [the meaning] come first.
Having surveyed the directions from the perspective of the surveying of directions,
one should indeed explain the discourse by means of the three methods, having condensed it with the hook.
3.3. The twelve-word phrase, the syllable, the phoneme,
the etymology, and likewise the exposition;
The statement "with the six aspects" includes all these syllables: revealing,
manifesting, and so forth.
"Exposition, analysis, making clear, and description of action—
by these six terms,
both the meaning and the action are demonstrated."
The three methods are complete,
and the six steps of the meaning have been calculated;
by means of nine phrases, [the teaching] of the Blessed One—
The meaning of the words is well-combined;
there are nine ways of presenting the meaning and twenty-four ways of investigating the phrasing.
Combining both together,
there are thirty-three such guides.
This concludes the section on exposition.
